analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest Wall Street banks to publish detailed annual reports on their misconduct, executive pay, branch closures, forced arbitration, and fossil fuel financing.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote or a single Republican cosponsor, so the largest Wall Street banks were never required to publish the annual transparency reports it demanded.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the biggest, globally systemically important U.S. bank holding companies — firms like JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and Citigroup — to file a detailed annual report with the Federal Reserve each year. The report would cover enforcement actions against the bank and how many consumers, employees, or investors were harmed; employees fired for misconduct; executive pay versus median employee pay; use of forced arbitration clauses; trading desk profits; branch closures after mergers; whistleblower complaints; and climate matters, including financing for fossil fuel expansion and projects on indigenous or minority-community lands. The Federal Reserve would have to post the reports publicly. The bill was introduced in September 2024, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, bank employees, and investors would gain visibility into the conduct of the biggest banks: how many people were harmed in enforcement actions, how executives' pay compares to front-line workers' pay, where branches closed after mergers, how often the bank forces disputes into arbitration, and how much it finances fossil fuel expansion and projects affecting indigenous and minority communities. Community groups, journalists, and regulators could use the public reports to press for change. Minority depository institutions and community development financial institutions would get attention through required disclosure of bank partnerships with them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, bank employees, and transparency advocates

how_it_helps.text: Requires each global systemically important bank holding company to file an annual report to the Federal Reserve covering its size and subsidiaries, enforcement actions against it and how many consumers, employees, or investors were harmed, employees fired for misconduct, trading desk structure and profits, use of forced arbitration, executive pay compared to median employee pay, minimum-wage workers, and whistleblower complaints

The reports must also disclose climate-related matters: financed emissions targets, reliance on offsets, financing for fossil fuel expansion, and financing of projects in low-income, majority-minority, or indigenous areas

Reports must cover mergers and acquisitions, including resulting retail branch closures and changes in regional market concentration, and the Federal Reserve must publish each report publicly on its website

Because the reports are public, consumers, workers, investors, and journalists could see for the first time in one place how each giant bank treats its customers, its lowest-paid employees, and the climate

analysis.who_pays: The global systemically important banks themselves would bear the cost of compiling the reports — listing subsidiaries, breaking down pay by decile, describing trading desk structure and profit sources, and tracking climate and environmental financing. Banks would also face reputational exposure from public disclosure of misconduct, pay gaps, branch closures, and fossil fuel financing.
analysis.who_pays_short: The largest U.S. Wall Street banks

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires banks to report; it sets no new rules, penalties, or enforcement, so a bank could file a fully accurate report and nothing would change for consumers, employees, or the climate

The required disclosures would be costly to produce, including detailed trading desk data, decile-by-decile pay breakdowns, and projections of solvency effects under 3 degrees Celsius of warming, some of which are inherently speculative

Centralizing the reports at the Federal Reserve and publishing them online would give regulators and the public a detailed new window into bank operations, which opponents in the industry would argue invites politicized second-guessing of legitimate business decisions

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest: sunlight on the eight biggest banks' pay gaps, enforcement records, branch closures, and fossil fuel financing, at almost no cost to ordinary taxpayers. The costs fall mainly on the banks in compliance work, which is the point. The honest drawback is that disclosure alone has no teeth — a bank can file a truthful report about harming millions of consumers and face no consequence, so the bill informs the public rather than changing what banks do. Given that limitation, the bill was a reasonable transparency step whose biggest cost was the political capital spent on it, wasted when it died without action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2024, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The House introduced the bill on September 25, 2024 and referred it the same day to the Committee on Financial Services, which is the last recorded action
The bill received no committee vote and no floor vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025
Only three House Democrats cosponsored the bill, and no Republican did, so it never had a broad enough coalition to be scheduled

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest Wall Street banks are better off: they avoid a public annual accounting of their enforcement records, pay gaps, branch closures, arbitration practices, and fossil fuel financing, and no one else gained from the bill's death.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill on September 25, 2024 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: House Republicans (224 of 440 members)
against.role: House majority caucus in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan support that typically moves a bill out of committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's four supporters — the sponsor and three cosponsors — were all House Democrats, and no Republican backed it; with one-party sponsorship and a majorityRepublican committee, it never moved.

industries.industry: Global systemically important banks (the largest U.S. Wall Street bank holding companies)
industries.note: These banks would have to compile and publish detailed annual reports on their trading profits, executive pay gaps, enforcement records, forced arbitration, branch closures, and fossil fuel financing. The information itself is the product: much of it is currently scattered, and publicizing it exposes the banks to reputational and political pressure, which is why their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the public's interest in seeing it.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel companies and extraction projects financed by big banks
industries.note: The bill would not restrict fossil fuel financing; it would only require banks to disclose how much they lend to fossil fuel expansion and to projects on indigenous or minority-community lands. The financing itself continues unchanged; only its visibility increases.
